title: Chapter 08: TCP & UDP Programming
description: Master Java Socket API programming for TCP (connection-oriented, reliable byte streams) and UDP (connectionless datagrams, unicast, broadcast, and multicast), framing strategies, ncat debugging, messaging patterns, service discovery, and interactive REPLs.

sections.title: 1. The Socket API & TCP Stream Semantics
sections.description: Understand how the Berkeley Socket API abstracts network communication in Java and why TCP is a reliable byte stream rather than a message protocol.

blocks.title: The Socket API & TCP Stream Semantics
blocks.content:
Java's **Socket API** (`java.net`) exposes transport-layer communication like a file: **open** (connect/accept), **read** (`InputStream`), **write** (`OutputStream`), and **close**—decorated with UTF-8 `BufferedReader`/`BufferedWriter` just like file I/O.

**TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)** defines four core properties:
* **Connection-oriented:** Endpoints perform a handshake before exchanging application data bidirectionally.
* **Unicast only:** Links **exactly two** applications (5 servers = 5 separate TCP connections).
* **Reliable & Ordered:** Segments are numbered with **sequence numbers**; lost segments are retransmitted and out-of-order segments are reassembled. Broken connections throw `IOException`.
* **Stream-oriented (NOT Message-Oriented):** The #1 exam trap in TCP programming.

> [!WARNING]
> **Exam Trap — `write()` != `read()`:**
> If a client calls `out.write("HELLO")` then `out.write("WORLD")`, TCP does **not** preserve boundaries. The server's `read()` may receive `"HELLOWORLD"` in one call, or `"HEL"`, `"LOWO"`, `"RLD"` across three calls. Your application protocol **must** add framing (e.g., `\n` delimiter or length prefix).

blocks.title: TCP Byte Stream vs UDP Datagram Boundaries
blocks.caption: TCP treats data as a continuous byte stream requiring application-level framing (such as \n), whereas UDP preserves discrete datagram boundaries.
blocks.source:
flowchart LR
  subgraph TCP ["TCP: Continuous Byte Stream"]
    TW1["write('HI\\n')"] --> TStream["Byte Stream: H I \\n B Y E \\n"]
    TW2["write('BYE\\n')"] --> TStream
    TStream --> TR1["read() -> 'HI\\nBY'"]
    TStream --> TR2["read() -> 'E\\n'"]
    TR1 --> TFrame["App Framing (readLine) reconstructs 'HI' & 'BYE'"]
    TR2 --> TFrame
  end

  subgraph UDP ["UDP: Discrete Datagrams"]
    UW1["send('HI')"] --> UD1["Datagram 1: 'HI'"]
    UW2["send('BYE')"] --> UD2["Datagram 2: 'BYE'"]
    UD1 --> UR1["receive() -> 'HI'"]
    UD2 --> UR2["receive() -> 'BYE'"]
  end

  classDef tcpNode fill:#e0e7ff,stroke:#4f46e5,stroke-width:1.5px;
  classDef udpNode fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#059669,stroke-width:1.5px;

blocks.title: ServerSocket vs Socket & The OS Backlog Queue
blocks.content:
Java separates the roles of listening for connections and communicating over an established connection into two classes:

| Class | Role | Key Behavior & Failure Modes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `ServerSocket(port)` | **Server listener** | Binds to `port` and starts listening immediately. Throws `BindException: Address already in use` if another process already holds that port. |
| `serverSocket.accept()` | **Accepts one client** | **Blocks** until a client connects, then returns a new `Socket` dedicated to that client. `serverSocket` stays open to accept future clients. |
| `new Socket(host, port)` | **Client connector** | Initiates the TCP connection (blocking). The OS picks an ephemeral local port for the client. Throws `ConnectException: Connection refused` if no server is listening. |

### Crucial Subtlety: What Happens Before `accept()`?
As soon as `new ServerSocket(6430)` runs, the **operating system** begins accepting incoming TCP handshakes into a **pending connection queue** (whose size is controlled by the `backlog` parameter).

That means a client's `new Socket("localhost", 6430)` can succeed *even while the server is still busy serving a previous client and hasn't called `accept()` yet*! The client's sent bytes are buffered by the server's OS kernel until the server finally calls `accept()` and reads from the newly returned `Socket`.

### Detecting Connection Closure
When the client calls `socket.close()`, TCP sends a FIN segment. On the server side, `BufferedReader.readLine()` returns **`null`** (end-of-stream / EOF). The server then closes its client `Socket` and loops back to `accept()`.

blocks.title: TCP Client/Server Lifecycle Sequence
blocks.caption: Complete lifecycle from ServerSocket binding and OS backlog queueing to accept(), framed line exchange, and graceful EOF closure.
blocks.source:
sequenceDiagram
  participant S as Server App
  participant OS as Server OS Kernel
  participant C as Client App

  S->>OS: new ServerSocket(6430)
  Note over OS: Listening on port 6430
  S->>OS: serverSocket.accept() [BLOCKS]
  C->>OS: new Socket("localhost", 6430)
  OS-->>C: TCP Handshake Complete
  OS-->>S: Returns dedicated client Socket
  C->>S: write("Hello\\n") + flush()
  S->>C: readLine() -> "Hello" -> write("Hello\\n") + flush()
  C->>OS: socket.close() [FIN]
  OS-->>S: readLine() returns null (EOF)
  S->>S: clientSocket.close(), loop to accept()
  S->>OS: serverSocket.close()

sections.title: 2. Processing TCP Streams, Echo Server & ncat Debugging
sections.description: Decorate socket streams with UTF-8 buffered readers/writers, avoid the missing-flush and missing-newline traps, and debug protocols using ncat.

blocks.title: Decorating Streams, Flushing, and Variable-Length Framing
blocks.content:
Raw `socket.getInputStream()` and `socket.getOutputStream()` only read and write `byte`s. For text protocols, always decorate them with explicit UTF-8 encoding and buffering:

```java
BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(
    new InputStreamReader(socket.getInputStream(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
BufferedWriter out = new BufferedWriter(
    new OutputStreamWriter(socket.getOutputStream(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
```

### Two Golden Rules for Text Protocols
1. **Always terminate messages with `\n`:** `BufferedReader.readLine()` blocks until it sees a line terminator (`\n` or `\r\n`) or EOF. If you send `out.write("Hello")` without `\n`, the peer's `readLine()` will **hang forever**.
2. **Always call `out.flush()`:** `BufferedWriter` holds characters in memory until its internal buffer (typically 8 KB) fills up or the stream is closed. Without `out.flush()`, small messages sit in RAM and never reach the network.

### Framing Variable-Length Data
When messages can span multiple lines or arbitrary lengths, two standard framing strategies are used:
* **Explicit Delimiter:** Read lines until a sentinel like End-of-Transmission (`String EOT = "\u0004";`) is encountered.
* **Length Prefix:** Send a header line first (e.g., `DATA_LENGTH 42\n`), parse the integer `42`, then read exactly `42` characters via `in.read()`.

blocks.title: Debugging Broken Protocols with ncat
blocks.content:
When a TCP client and server hang, both sides might be waiting on `readLine()`. `ncat` isolates which side is at fault by replacing either peer:

```bash
# Replace the client: type lines manually and watch the server
ncat localhost 6430

# Replace the server: inspect raw bytes sent by the client
ncat -l 6430
```

### Diagnosing Missing `\n` and `flush()` Bugs
Suppose a buggy TCP client and server both omit `"\n"` and `out.flush()`:
1. **Client vs `ncat -l 6430`:** Nothing appears in `ncat` while the client runs! Only when the client exits and `try-with-resources` closes `out` does the buffer flush, printing `Hello 1Hello 2Hello 3` glued onto a single line.
2. **`ncat localhost 6430` vs Server:** The server prints `Received: ...` for each line you type, but `ncat` receives nothing back until you press `Ctrl+D` (EOF). Closing the server's `out` flushes all echoed lines glued together.

**Fix on both sides:** Change `out.write(line)` to `out.write(line + "\n")` followed by `out.flush()`.

sections.title: 3. UDP Datagrams & Reliability Trade-offs
sections.description: Contrast TCP streams with connectionless UDP datagrams, understand IPv4 payload limits and fragmentation, and explore when applications tolerate or rebuild reliability.

blocks.title: UDP Datagrams: The Postcard Analogy
blocks.content:
**UDP (User Datagram Protocol)** is a minimalist, **connectionless** transport protocol. Think of it like sending **postcards**:
* You write a destination address and message on each postcard and drop it in the mailbox—no handshake or connection setup.
* Postcards travel independently: one may arrive out of order, or get lost entirely, with no automatic retransmission.

### Datagram Structure & The 65,507-Byte Limit
Each UDP **datagram** is a self-contained chunk with a header (source port, destination port, length, checksum) and a payload:

$$\text{Max UDP Payload} = 65{,}535\text{ B (16-bit IPv4 length)} - 20\text{ B (IPv4 header)} - 8\text{ B (UDP header)} = 65{,}507\text{ bytes}$$

> [!WARNING]
> **Fragmentation & Silent Truncation Pitfalls:**
> 1. **All-or-Nothing IP Fragmentation:** If a datagram exceeds the network MTU (typically 1500 bytes), IP splits it into fragments. If *even one* fragment is lost, IP discards the entire datagram.
> 2. **Undersized Receive Buffer:** If your Java `byte[] buffer` is smaller than the incoming datagram, `DatagramSocket.receive()` **silently truncates** the extra bytes! Always size your buffer from the application protocol specification (e.g., 256 or 1024 bytes depending on maximum message size).

blocks.title: When to Use UDP & How Applications Handle Loss
Interactive Simulation: IP Fragmentation & UDP Datagram Survival Rate

Adjust the number of IP fragments N and per-fragment network loss probability p (%) to observe how datagram survival collapses for oversized UDP payloads.

sections.title: 4. Unicast, Broadcast & Multicast Topologies
sections.description: Compare one-to-one, one-to-all, and one-to-many UDP delivery, compute subnet broadcast addresses, and implement MulticastSocket receivers.

blocks.title: Unicast vs Broadcast vs Multicast
blocks.content:
Unlike TCP (which only supports unicast), UDP supports three communication modes:

| Feature | Unicast (1-to-1) | Broadcast (1-to-All) | Multicast (1-to-Many) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Analogy** | Private conversation | Public PA announcement | Radio / Discord channel |
| **Receivers** | One specific host | All hosts on local subnet | Only hosts that joined the group |
| **Destination IP** | Receiver's IP | `255.255.255.255` or subnet broadcast | `224.0.0.0`–`239.255.255.255` (use `239.x.x.x` locally; IPv6 `ff00::/8`) |
| **Receiver Setup** | Bound to port | Bound to port | Bound to port **+** `joinGroup()` |
| **Crosses Routers?** | Yes | No (local network only) | Only with multicast routing; almost never on public Internet |
| **Supported by TCP?** | Yes | No | No |

### Computing a Subnet Broadcast Address
Take the **bitwise OR** of the network address and the **bitwise NOT** of the subnet mask (`network_IP | ~mask`). For `172.16.0.0/12`:
1. **Network IP:** `172.16.0.0` (`10101100.00010000.00000000.00000000`)
2. **Mask `/12`:** `255.240.0.0` → **NOT Mask:** `0.15.255.255`
3. **Broadcast (OR):** `172.31.255.255`

Universal local broadcast: `255.255.255.255`. Local multicast apps (RFC 2365): **`239.0.0.0`–`239.255.255.255`**.

blocks.title: UDP in Java's Socket API: DatagramSocket, DatagramPacket & MulticastSocket
blocks.content:
UDP replaces `ServerSocket`/`Socket` with three classes:

* **`DatagramSocket`:** Used by both emitters and receivers. Receivers bind a known port (`new DatagramSocket(4445)`); emitters can let the OS choose an ephemeral port (`new DatagramSocket()`).
* **`DatagramPacket`:** Wraps a `byte[]` payload. When **sending**, pass destination `InetAddress` and `port`. When **receiving**, pass an empty `byte[]` buffer and its length.
* **`MulticastSocket`:** Subclass of `DatagramSocket` for receivers calling `joinGroup(group, netIf)` / `leaveGroup(group, netIf)` on a specific `NetworkInterface` (e.g., `eth0`, `en0`).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Exam Traps vs TCP:**
> - **No `accept()`** and **no connection state**.
> - `socket.send(packet)` **returns immediately**, even if no receiver is listening.
> - `socket.close()` sends **nothing** over the network—the peer is never notified.
> - Java enables `SO_BROADCAST` by default, though `socket.setBroadcast(true)` states intent explicitly.

blocks.title: Annotated UDP Multicast Emitter & Receiver

annotations.note: The emitter only needs an ordinary DatagramSocket—it does NOT need to join the multicast group.
Targets the local administratively scoped multicast address 239.0.0.0 on port 4446.
The receiver binds a MulticastSocket to port 4446.

blocks.title: Sandbox: Fix the DatagramPacket.setLength() Reuse Bug
blocks.instructions: When reusing a single `DatagramPacket` across multiple `receive()` calls, Java's `receive()` mutates `packet.length` down to the size of the *previous* datagram! Without resetting `packet.setLength(buffer.length)` before each receive, subsequent longer datagrams get silently truncated. Run the starter code to observe the bug (`"TEMPERATURE 22.5"` truncated to 2 bytes `"TE"`), then fix it in `Main`.
blocks.expected_output:
Received [2]: HI
Received [16]: TEMPERATURE 22.5
Received [2]: OK
hints: Look at `packet.getLength()` inside `simulateReceive`: after `"HI"` arrives, `packet.getLength()` is `2`.
Call `packet.setLength(buffer.length);` right before `simulateReceive(packet, msg);` (or create a fresh `DatagramPacket` each iteration).

sections.title: 5. Messaging Patterns, Service Discovery & Interactive REPLs
sections.description: Design fire-and-forget vs request-response exchanges, bootstrap unknown server IPs with UDP service discovery, and keep connections alive with a REPL.

blocks.title: UDP Messaging Patterns & Multi-Emitter Behavior
blocks.content:
Because UDP has no built-in session model, your application defines its messaging pattern:

1. **Fire-and-Forget:** One-way communication. An emitter sends a datagram and never expects an acknowledgement or reply (e.g., periodic sensor readings).
2. **Request-Response (Request-Reply):** Two-way communication. Every received `DatagramPacket` carries the sender's IP (`packet.getAddress()`) and port (`packet.getPort()`). The receiver extracts these to send a **unicast** reply back to the exact requester.

### Single-Threaded TCP vs UDP Concurrency
* **TCP Server:** A single-threaded TCP server loops inside `while ((line = in.readLine()) != null)` for Client 1. Until Client 1 disconnects, the server never returns to `accept()`, so Client 2 sits waiting in the OS backlog queue (multi-threading solves this by spawning a handler per accepted `Socket`).
* **UDP Receiver:** A single `DatagramSocket` has **no connection state**. Every `receive()` simply returns the next incoming datagram regardless of which emitter sent it—so multiple UDP emitters work out of the box with one receiver socket!

blocks.title: Service Discovery Protocols: Advertisement vs Query
blocks.content:
How can a client connect to a server if it doesn't know the server's IP address in advance? Unicast cannot help—but **broadcast** and **multicast** only require a pre-agreed port (and group address) known to all participants.

Service discovery uses broadcast/multicast for the **first** message, then switches to **unicast** (UDP or TCP) using the discovered IP and port:

| Pattern | Who Speaks First? | Mechanism | Best For |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Advertisement** (Passive) | **Service Provider** (Server) | Periodically broadcasts/multicasts its service info (name, IP, port). Consumers listen passively. | Discovering all available services & detecting when one goes offline. |
| **Query** (Active) | **Service Consumer** (Client) | Broadcasts/multicasts a discovery query. Matching providers reply in **unicast** (request-response). | On-demand lookup without constant background network chatter. |

blocks.title: Annotated Interactive REPL Server Loop

annotations.note: Keeps the TCP connection open across multiple commands until the client disconnects (null) or sends QUIT.
Explicit exit command lets the client or server terminate the REPL cleanly.
Breaks out of the REPL loop so try-with-resources can close the socket and return to accept().
Always end every REPL response with \n and flush() so the client's readLine() unblocks.

blocks.title: Complete TCP vs UDP Comparison
blocks.content:
| Dimension | TCP | UDP |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Connection model** | Connection-oriented (`ServerSocket` / `Socket`) | Connectionless (`DatagramSocket` / `DatagramPacket`) |
| **Reliability** | Reliable (retransmission, ordering, error on drop) | Unreliable (may drop, duplicate, or reorder) |
| **Data abstraction** | Continuous **byte stream** (needs framing) | Discrete **datagrams** (max 65,507 B IPv4 payload) |
| **Communication modes** | Unicast only | Unicast, Broadcast, and Multicast |
| **Messaging patterns** | Typically Request-Response / REPL | Fire-and-Forget, Request-Response |
| **Service discovery** | Not suitable directly | Ideal (Broadcast / Multicast Advertisement & Query) |
| **Typical protocols** | HTTP, SMTP, FTP, SSH | DNS, live streaming, multiplayer gaming (e.g. Factorio) |

sections.title: 6. Exam Bug Synthesis
sections.description: Diagnose the two highest-yield Java TCP/UDP implementation bugs in your own words.

blocks.title: Synthesis: Stream Buffering vs Datagram Reuse
blocks.prompt: Compare two classic Java networking bugs: (1) calling `out.write("Hello")` on a TCP `BufferedWriter` without `\n` or `flush()`, and (2) reusing a UDP `DatagramPacket` in a `receive()` loop without calling `packet.setLength(buffer.length)`. Explain what symptom each bug produces and why.
self_check_criteria: Explained that BufferedWriter holds bytes in an in-memory buffer until full, flushed, or closed—causing the peer to hang.
Explained that BufferedReader.readLine() blocks until a newline delimiter (\n) or EOF arrives.
Explained that DatagramSocket.receive() overwrites packet.length with the received datagram's byte count, silently truncating any larger subsequent datagram unless reset.
blocks.model_answer: In the TCP bug, omitting flush() traps 'Hello' inside BufferedWriter's RAM buffer so no bytes hit the wire until the stream closes; even if flushed, omitting '\n' leaves the peer's readLine() blocking forever waiting for a line delimiter. In the UDP bug, receive() mutates the DatagramPacket's internal length field to match the incoming datagram size (e.g., 2 bytes). On the next loop iteration, receive() only allows up to 2 bytes into the buffer, silently truncating longer messages unless packet.setLength(buffer.length) resets the capacity.

sections.title: 7. Diagnostic Knowledge Check
sections.description: Test your understanding of TCP stream semantics, Socket API mechanics, UDP datagrams, subnet broadcast math, multicast, and service discovery.

blocks.title: TCP Message Boundaries
blocks.question: A TCP client calls `out.write("PING")` followed immediately by `out.write("PONG")` (and flushes). What is guaranteed when the server calls `in.read()`?
options: The server is guaranteed to receive the bytes `P-I-N-G-P-O-N-G` in order, though they may arrive in one read or split across multiple reads.
The server's first `read()` is guaranteed to return `"PING"` and its second `read()` is guaranteed to return `"PONG"`.
The server will drop `"PONG"` if it arrives before the first `read()` completes.
The server must call `ServerSocket.accept()` twice—once for `"PING"` and once for `"PONG"`.
blocks.correct_answer: The server is guaranteed to receive the bytes `P-I-N-G-P-O-N-G` in order, though they may arrive in one read or split across multiple reads.
blocks.explanation:
TCP is a reliable, ordered **byte stream**, not a message-oriented protocol. It guarantees all bytes arrive in order without loss, but it does NOT preserve `write()` boundaries—your application must add framing (such as `\n`).

* Claiming two `read()` calls return `"PING"` and `"PONG"` confuses TCP with UDP datagrams.
* TCP never silently drops bytes on a healthy connection.
* `accept()` is called once per client connection, not once per message.
hints: Does TCP preserve application `write()` boundaries, or does it treat data as a continuous stream?
Think about how TCP sequence numbers reassemble bytes rather than messages.

blocks.title: Client Connecting Before accept()
blocks.question: A single-threaded TCP server is busy inside a `while` loop serving Client A. Meanwhile, Client B runs `new Socket("localhost", 6430)` and sends `"Hello\n"`. What happens immediately on Client B?
options: The OS kernel accepts the TCP handshake into the server's backlog queue, so `new Socket(...)` succeeds and `"Hello\n"` is buffered by the server's OS until `accept()` is called.
Client B immediately throws `ConnectException: Connection refused` because the server is not currently inside `accept()`.
Client B's `new Socket(...)` throws `BindException: Address already in use`.
Client B's `"Hello\n"` is delivered directly into Client A's `BufferedReader`.
blocks.correct_answer: The OS kernel accepts the TCP handshake into the server's backlog queue, so `new Socket(...)` succeeds and `"Hello\n"` is buffered by the server's OS until `accept()` is called.
blocks.explanation:
As soon as `new ServerSocket(6430)` is created, the OS listens and queues incoming connections up to the `backlog` limit. Client B's handshake completes at the OS level and its data is buffered until the server calls `accept()`.

* `Connection refused` only happens if no `ServerSocket` is bound to port 6430.
* `Address already in use` occurs when binding a `ServerSocket` to an occupied port.
* Each client gets its own `Socket` instance; data never leaks into Client A's stream.
hints: Who actually performs the TCP 3-way handshake when `ServerSocket` is listening—your Java loop or the OS kernel?
Remember the `backlog` queue parameter on `ServerSocket`.

blocks.title: Diagnosing Missing `\n` and `flush()` with `ncat -l 6430`
blocks.question: You run a TCP client that calls `out.write("Hello " + i)` three times in a `try-with-resources` block without appending `\n` or calling `flush()`, targeting `ncat -l 6430`. What does `ncat` display while the client is running and right as it exits?
options: Nothing appears while the client runs; when the client closes its streams on exit, `ncat` prints `Hello 1Hello 2Hello 3` on a single line.
`ncat` prints `Hello 1`, `Hello 2`, and `Hello 3` on three separate lines immediately.
`ncat` prints `Hello 1` immediately, then hangs on `Hello 2`.
`ncat` throws `SocketTimeoutException` after 2 seconds.
blocks.correct_answer: Nothing appears while the client runs; when the client closes its streams on exit, `ncat` prints `Hello 1Hello 2Hello 3` on a single line.
blocks.explanation:
Without `flush()`, `BufferedWriter` buffers all three writes in RAM. When the client exits its `try-with-resources` block, closing the `BufferedWriter` flushes the buffer—and because no `\n` was written, all three strings appear glued together as `Hello 1Hello 2Hello 3`.

* Immediate printing only happens if `flush()` is called.
* `ncat` does not have a 2-second `SocketTimeoutException` by default.
hints: Where do the characters live after `BufferedWriter.write(...)` if `flush()` is not called?
What happens to a `BufferedWriter` when `try-with-resources` closes it?

blocks.title: Maximum IPv4 UDP Payload Size
blocks.question: An IPv4 packet has a maximum total length of 65,535 bytes (16-bit field). Given a 20-byte IPv4 header and an 8-byte UDP header, what is the maximum UDP payload size?
options: 65,507 bytes
65,527 bytes
65,515 bytes
1,500 bytes
blocks.explanation:
Subtract both headers from the 65,535-byte IPv4 limit: $65{,}535 - 20 - 8 = 65{,}507$ bytes.

* `65,527` forgets to subtract the 20-byte IPv4 header.
* `65,515` forgets to subtract the 8-byte UDP header.
* `1,500` is a typical Ethernet MTU, above which IP *fragments* the packet rather than forbidding it.
hints: Start from 65,535 and subtract both the IPv4 header (20 B) and UDP header (8 B).

blocks.title: Predict Output: Reused DatagramPacket Without Reset
options: HE
HELLO
OK
HEO
blocks.explanation:
The first call `simulateReceive(p, "OK")` sets `p.length` to `2`. Because `p.setLength(buf.length)` is NOT called before the second receive, `p.getLength()` is still `2`, so `"HELLO"` is silently truncated to its first 2 bytes: `"HE"`.

* `HELLO` would only print if `p.setLength(buf.length)` were called.
* `OK` is overwritten by the first 2 bytes of `HELLO`.
hints: What is `p.getLength()` after the first `simulateReceive(p, "OK")` completes?
How many bytes will the second `simulateReceive` accept if `p.length` is not reset?

blocks.title: Computing a Subnet Broadcast Address
blocks.question: What is the broadcast address for the IPv4 subnet `192.168.10.0/24` (subnet mask `255.255.255.0`)?
blocks.explanation:
The `/24` mask (`255.255.255.0`) has a bitwise NOT of `0.0.0.255`. Taking the bitwise OR with `192.168.10.0` sets all 8 host bits to `1`, yielding `192.168.10.255`.

* `192.168.255.255` corresponds to a `/16` mask.
* `192.168.10.0` is the network address itself.
* `192.168.10.1` is typically the default gateway.
hints: With `/24`, the first 3 octets are fixed as the network prefix and the last octet (8 bits) is the host suffix.
Set all host bits to `1` (255).

blocks.title: Multicast Characteristics
blocks.question: Which of the following statements about IPv4 UDP Multicast are true? (Select all that apply)
options: Addresses in `239.0.0.0` to `239.255.255.255` are reserved for local administratively scoped applications.
A multicast receiver must use `MulticastSocket` and call `joinGroup(group, netIf)` to receive datagrams sent to the group.
Multicast works reliably across the public Internet without any VPN or special router configuration.
A multicast emitter can send to the group using a standard `DatagramSocket` without joining the group.
correct_answer: Addresses in `239.0.0.0` to `239.255.255.255` are reserved for local administratively scoped applications.
A multicast receiver must use `MulticastSocket` and call `joinGroup(group, netIf)` to receive datagrams sent to the group.
A multicast emitter can send to the group using a standard `DatagramSocket` without joining the group.
blocks.explanation: RFC 2365 reserves `239.0.0.0/8` for local multicast apps. Receivers use `MulticastSocket.joinGroup(...)` on a `NetworkInterface`, while emitters just send `DatagramPacket`s to the group address. Multicast is almost never routed across the public Internet without a tunnel/VPN.
hints: Recall RFC 2365 for local multicast addressing.
Does an emitter need to subscribe to a radio channel to broadcast on it, or only the listeners?

blocks.title: Sending UDP When No Server Is Listening
blocks.question: A UDP client creates a `DatagramSocket` and calls `socket.send(packet)` targeting port 4445, where no receiver is running. What happens?
options: `socket.send(packet)` returns immediately without throwing an exception.
`socket.send(packet)` throws `ConnectException: Connection refused`.
`socket.send(packet)` blocks until a receiver starts on port 4445.
The client's `DatagramSocket` automatically switches to broadcast mode.
blocks.correct_answer: `socket.send(packet)` returns immediately without throwing an exception.
blocks.explanation:
UDP is connectionless and fire-and-forget at the transport layer: `send()` simply hands the datagram to the OS network stack and returns immediately, even if nobody is listening.

* `Connection refused` on connect is a TCP behavior.
* `receive()` blocks, not `send()`.
hints: Does UDP perform a handshake before `send()`?
Think of dropping a postcard into a mailbox—does the mailbox check if anyone is home?

blocks.title: Advertisement vs Query Service Discovery
blocks.question: In an **active (Query)** service discovery protocol, what is the sequence of communication?
options: The consumer broadcasts/multicasts a query to a pre-agreed port/group, and available providers reply in unicast with their connection details.
The provider periodically broadcasts its presence while consumers listen passively.
The consumer opens a TCP connection to `255.255.255.255` and calls `accept()`.
The provider sends a unicast packet to every IP on the Internet.
blocks.correct_answer: The consumer broadcasts/multicasts a query to a pre-agreed port/group, and available providers reply in unicast with their connection details.
blocks.explanation:
In a **Query** (active) pattern, the consumer speaks first via broadcast or multicast to a known port/group. Providers listening there extract the consumer's IP and port from the `DatagramPacket` and reply in unicast.

* Periodic announcements by the provider describe the **Advertisement** (passive) pattern.
* TCP does not support broadcast.
hints: Who speaks first in an *active* (Query) protocol—the consumer or the provider?
How does the provider respond once it receives the query?

blocks.title: Single-Threaded TCP Server vs UDP Receiver with Multiple Clients
blocks.question: Why can a single-threaded UDP receiver (`while (true) socket.receive(p)`) immediately process messages from 5 concurrent emitters, whereas a single-threaded TCP REPL server blocks Client 2 until Client 1 disconnects?
options: UDP has no connection state and reads all incoming datagrams from one `DatagramSocket`; the single-threaded TCP server stays trapped in Client 1's `readLine()` loop before it can call `accept()` again.
UDP automatically spawns a new Java thread per emitter inside `DatagramSocket`.
TCP limits `ServerSocket` to a maximum of 1 connection for the lifetime of the JVM.
UDP packets bypass the operating system kernel.
blocks.correct_answer: UDP has no connection state and reads all incoming datagrams from one `DatagramSocket`; the single-threaded TCP server stays trapped in Client 1's `readLine()` loop before it can call `accept()` again.
blocks.explanation: A UDP receiver uses a single connectionless `DatagramSocket`—every `receive()` returns the next datagram from any emitter. A single-threaded TCP server has one `Socket` per client and stays inside Client 1's loop until EOF (`null`), starving Client 2 in the backlog queue until `accept()` is called again.
hints: Compare how many sockets are involved on the server/receiver side in TCP vs UDP.
What prevents the single-threaded TCP server from reaching `serverSocket.accept()`?

sections.title: 8. Spaced Repetition Flashcards
sections.description: High-yield API, CLI, and formula flashcards that complement (without duplicating) the diagnostic quiz.

blocks.title: `ServerSocket` vs `Socket`
blocks.front: What is the difference between `ServerSocket` and `Socket` in Java?
blocks.back: `ServerSocket` binds a port and listens for incoming connections; `accept()` blocks and returns a dedicated `Socket` for each client. `Socket` represents a connected endpoint (used by both the client and the server's accepted client handler).
blocks.hint: One listens for connections; the other carries data.

blocks.title: Debugging with `ncat`
blocks.front: What `ncat` commands replace (a) a TCP client and (b) a TCP server on port `6430`?

blocks.title: Preventing Infinite `receive()` Blocking
blocks.front: How do you prevent `DatagramSocket.receive()` from blocking forever when a UDP packet or reply is lost?
blocks.back: Call `socket.setSoTimeout(ms)` (e.g., `2000` ms) and catch `SocketTimeoutException` to retry or abort.

blocks.title: Broadcast Addressing
blocks.front: What is the universal local broadcast IP, and how do you compute a specific subnet's broadcast address?
blocks.back:
Universal local broadcast: `255.255.255.255`.
Subnet broadcast: `network_IP | (~subnet_mask)` (bitwise OR of network address with bitwise NOT of mask).
